recentEmptyResults.title: 2 · Investigate flow vulnerabilities
recentEmptyResults.explanation:
The flow works as the lead describes, but it does not show a vulnerability.

1. Only the owner can use the approval. A ticket owner can approve a second RaffleFactory deployment and escrow their own ticket of raffle T as the prize of that factory's clone C2. T._update only checks T's own factory, and that scope is documented ("same-factory protocol plumbing", Raffle.sol:587-605). The approval cannot be used against the owner by anyone else. RaffleFactory.createRaffle always uses msg.sender both as the transfer `from` (RaffleFactory.sol:128) and as the clone's sponsor (line 112). ERC721.transferFrom reverts unless the previous owner equals `from` (ERC721.sol:121-124), and C2.onERC721Received requires from == sponsor (Raffle.sol:423). If a third party called F2.createRaffle with the victim's ticket, it would revert with ERC721IncorrectOwner.

2. The ticket is never stranded. It becomes C2's configured prize, and C2 always reaches a state where it can release it:
   - In NftWon, the C2 winner calls redeemWinningTicket, which runs prizeToken.transferFrom(C2, winner, id) (Raffle.sol:334).
   - In CashWon or Refunding, anyone can call releaseSponsorPrize (Raffle.sol:404).
   - Permissionless enableRefunds deadlines guarantee C2 reaches one of these states (Raffle.sol:276-301).

3. T loses nothing. T's own claim paths have no expiry: refundTickets, redeemWinningTicket, and the permissionless, ownership-independent settleWinningTicket (Raffle.sol:304-372). So T's sponsor, its treasury and its other ticket holders keep full access to their proceeds, fees, refunds and prize return while the ticket is escrowed. The only effect is that the actor's own claim is delayed or exposed to C2's outcome. The actor chose this, much like listing an NFT in any escrow contract.

4. The remaining lock-up cases all need the actor's own choices, such as setting C2's sponsorRecipient to an address T rejects. They only affect the actor's own claim.

No third party loses funds, no accounting breaks, and no unauthorized transfer is possible.

recentEmptyResults.title: 2 · Investigate flow vulnerabilities
recentEmptyResults.explanation: No exploitable vulnerability in this flow. The reentry is real, but it gives the hook contract no power beyond what it already has. (1) Raffle.sol:235 _safeMint reaches the recipient's onERC721Received through ERC721.sol:289 and ERC721Utils.sol:33. From there the only state-changing functions that are not guarded are the inherited ERC721 approve, setApprovalForAll, transferFrom and safeTransferFrom. These check normal owner/operator authority (_setApprovalForAll(_msgSender()), _checkAuthorized), so the hook can only approve or move tickets it already owns or is approved for. Every Raffle function that changes state is nonReentrant. initialize is blocked by the initialized flag. Raffle.onERC721Received requires AwaitingPrize, the prize token as caller and the factory as operator. rawFulfillRandomWords only accepts the VRF wrapper. (2) When the hook runs, buyEntries has already finished its accounting (totalEntries, ticketCount, _ticketRanges, unsettledPot, owner) and the values are consistent. Afterwards it only emits TicketPurchased from local variables. Nothing on-chain reads ticket ownership or approvals later in the transaction. _settleWinningTicket uses only the stored ranges. redeemWinningTicket and refundTickets check ownerOf again when they are called. A transfer made inside the hook still passes the Raffle.sol:497 _update check that blocks protocol addresses. (3) Moving a ticket inside the hook has the same effect as moving it right after buyEntries returns. Tickets are designed as transferable bearer claims, and the only tickets affected belong to the hook contract, so nobody else loses anything. TicketPurchased.recipient still correctly names the address that received the mint, because Transfer(0 -> recipient) is logged first. The workspace contains no indexer, subgraph or SDK code that treats TicketPurchased as current ownership, and DESIGN.md says frontend discovery is advisory and transactions must reread chain state. (4) The native refund call in requestDraw (Raffle.sol:267) runs after status, vrfRequestId and _requestInFlight are already set. The caller can only change its own tickets or make its own transaction revert.

recentEmptyResults.title: 2 · Investigate flow vulnerabilities
recentEmptyResults.explanation: No exploitable flaw in the setApprovalForAll / operator-transfer path. Raffle does not override setApprovalForAll, _setApprovalForAll, isApprovedForAll, _isAuthorized, _checkAuthorized or _approve. Its only ERC-721 override is _update (Raffle.sol:497-502), which screens the `to` address against protocol addresses and then calls super._update(to, ticketId, auth) with auth unchanged. So the OpenZeppelin 5.6.1 authorization logic is intact; the vendored files match dependency-hashes.json. Each transferFrom/safeTransferFrom re-reads _owners[ticketId] and checks _operatorApprovals[currentOwner][msg.sender] at call time (ERC721.sol:217-221, 164-187). Revoking takes effect immediately, an ownership change removes the old approver's operators, and per-token approvals are cleared on every transfer and burn (ERC721.sol:227). A burned or never-minted ticket can't be revived through the from==0 branch: _isAuthorized(address(0), ...) can never be true. Owner 0 is rejected at ERC721.sol:410, msg.sender is never zero, and _tokenApprovals can only be written for owned tokens and is zeroed on burn. Ticket IDs are sequential and never re-minted, so refunded or redeemed tickets can't be reused even though their ranges stay stored. A stale `from` reverts with ERC721IncorrectOwner after _update, which undoes the whole call. refundTickets and redeemWinningTicket require msg.sender == ownerOf(ticketId) (Raffle.sol:320-321, 359-360), so an operator only gets the transfer authority the owner granted. Approvals live in each clone's own storage, so nothing carries over between raffles. Operators regaining control of tickets that come back to or are minted to the approver is standard ERC-721 'all assets' behavior; a third party minting to the approver pays for that ticket. An operator-set per-token approval surviving revocation is also standard EIP-721/OZ behavior, needs an operator the victim already trusted, and is not specific to this project.

recentEmptyResults.title: 2 · Investigate flow vulnerabilities
recentEmptyResults.explanation: No exploitable issue in this flow. setApprovalForAll is the unmodified OpenZeppelin 5.6 function (ERC721.sol:105 -> _setApprovalForAll at :409-417). It only writes _operatorApprovals[msg.sender][operator], so an account can only grant rights over its own tickets, and the operator cannot be address(0). Raffle never reads isApprovedForAll, getApproved, _isAuthorized or _checkAuthorized; grep finds no use in src/. The approval is only consumed by the inherited transferFrom, safeTransferFrom and approve. That is standard ERC-721 transfer power the owner chose to grant, and Raffle's _update override (Raffle.sol:497-502) still screens the destination of operator-initiated transfers. Every burn or payout path rechecks ownership against msg.sender. refundTickets (Raffle.sol:358-360) requires msg.sender == ownerOf(ticketId) for each id before _burn, and pays msg.sender. A duplicated id reverts on its second ownerOf, so there is no double count, and remainingRefundLiability is decremented with checked arithmetic. redeemWinningTicket (Raffle.sol:320-321) requires msg.sender == ownerOf before the burn and before delivering the NFT or cash, and it pays winner == msg.sender. Any settlement done inside it at :315 is rolled back by the NotTicketOwner revert, including when an operator wraps the call in try/catch. _burn passes auth = 0 (ERC721.sol:304), but it is reachable only after these owner checks. No other path burns tickets or pays on someone else's behalf. releaseSponsorProceeds, releaseProtocolFees and releaseSponsorPrize pay fixed recipients (sponsorRecipient or protocolTreasury). settleWinningTicket only writes storage and can select only the single ticket whose stored range contains winningEntry; ids that were never minted have range (0,0) and revert. Raffle never calls its own ticket-transfer functions, so approving the raffle, factory or prize token as an operator gives them nothing. The one leftover concern: a seller with a stale marketplace listing could have a winning ticket bought cheaply after resolution. That depends on how sellers manage off-chain orders, and the design explicitly keeps tickets transferable in every state, so it is not a contract defect.

recentEmptyResults.title: 2 · Investigate flow vulnerabilities
recentEmptyResults.explanation: I found no concrete, exploitable vulnerability in the setApprovalForAll → operator transferFrom/safeTransferFrom → Raffle._update path. setApprovalForAll is unmodified OpenZeppelin code. Every transfer still reaches ERC721._update → _checkAuthorized with auth = msg.sender. Raffle's screen at Raffle.sol:498 only adds reverts and changes no state. The only paths that skip authorization (auth = 0) are _mint in buyEntries and _burn in redeem/refund; _transfer and _safeTransfer are never used. The screen's external calls are view calls to the immutable, trusted factory (an immutable getter and a mapping getter), so neither can revert. It never calls the untrusted prize token, so the prize token cannot block transfers. The gaps the brief lists (code-less addresses such as the predictable next CREATE clone address, raffles from other factories, no screening of the operator) only let the owner, or an operator the owner chose and who could take the tickets anyway, strand that owner's own ticket. No one else loses anything. Settlement (settleWinningTicket) does not check who owns the ticket, so sponsor and treasury shares are still allocated and released if the winning ticket is stranded. In CashWon the sponsor gets the NFT back through releaseSponsorPrize, and other holders' refunds are unaffected. Approving a protocol contract as operator gives no confused-deputy path: the raffle only calls prizeToken.transferFrom with itself as the sender (from = address(this)). The factory only calls prize.safeTransferFrom with the caller as the sender (from = msg.sender), and the factory refuses its own raffles as prize tokens. A raffle is registered before any untrusted call, and createRaffle is nonReentrant, so a transfer cannot reach a fresh clone before it is in the registry.
